Net Income vs Free Cash Flow vs Owner FCF
charts.annotation: Owner FCF, where shown, is the DCF's series after SBC, interest income and lease principal.

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Tower Limited: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Tower Limited: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Tower Limited: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Tower Limited: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Tower Limited: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Tower Limited: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Tower Limited: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Tower Limited: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Tower Limited: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue

combinedRatio.title: Combined operating ratio, claims ratio & expense ratio
combinedRatio.content:
The combined operating ratio is claims costs plus management expenses, both as a percentage of net earned premium. Below 100% the underwriting book is profitable before investment income; above 100% premiums alone do not cover claims and running costs.

For Tower: the BAU (business-as-usual) claims ratio strips out large/one-off weather and catastrophe events, so it is the cleaner read on underlying underwriting performance. H1 FY2026's combined ratio jumped to 82.6% (from 69.7% H1 FY2025) and the BAU claims ratio to 44.3% (from 38.1%) — a mix of genuine claims-cost normalisation after a benign FY2025 and NZ$18.5m of large event claims (vs NZ$3.0m a year earlier). Management expense ratio has stayed flat near 31%, so the swing is entirely on the claims side.

What to watch:

  • Combined ratio trending back toward the ~74-79% FY2024/25 range, or staying elevated
  • BAU claims ratio versus the total claims ratio — the gap is large-event cost
  • Management expense ratio drifting up as premium growth slows

gwp.title: Gross written premium
gwp.content:
Gross written premium (GWP) is the total premium Tower has written in the period before reinsurance and before it is earned over the life of each policy — the insurer's equivalent of top-line sales volume.

For Tower: GWP growth has slowed sharply, from double digits in FY2023 to +2% in FY2025 and +1.3% H1 FY2026 vs H1 FY2025, as past years' large rate increases (used to restore margin after weather losses) work through and retention becomes the harder job. Compare GWP growth against the claims ratio: rate increases that outrun claims inflation are what rebuilt the combined ratio into FY2025.

What to watch:

  • GWP growth decomposed into rate versus policy count/retention where disclosed
  • Net earned premium lagging GWP (premium not yet earned)

largeEventClaims.title: Large event claims
largeEventClaims.content:
Large event claims are the cost of weather and catastrophe events large enough for Tower to disclose separately from ordinary (BAU) claims — cyclone, flood and severe storm losses that vary sharply year to year regardless of underlying underwriting quality.

For Tower: this is the single biggest swing factor behind H1 FY2026's profit decline: NZ$18.5m of large event claims versus NZ$3.0m in H1 FY2025 took a NZ$15.5m bite directly out of underlying profit after tax, which fell to NZ$36.8m from NZ$61.7m. The line was only broken out separately from H1 FY2025 onward, so earlier periods have no comparable figure.

What to watch:

  • Large event claims against Tower's full-year catastrophe allowance/reinsurance cover
  • Whether a bad half is an isolated weather event or a trend in event frequency
